title: Alan Alda reveals unexpected weapon in his battle against Parkinson's disease
excerpt: Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, said humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those ...
body_text:
Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, said humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.

Alan Alda is sharing his surprising method of coping with Parkinson’s.

The actor, 90, best known for portraying Captain Benjamin Franklin "Hawkeye" Pierce in the CBS wartime sitcom "M*A*S*H," was diagnosed with the degenerative motor disease in 2015 and publicly shared the news in 2018.

The diagnosis came after the actor learned that his own behavior of acting out dreams could be an early Parkinson's symptom.

DAD JOKES MAY BE GOOD FOR YOUR BRAIN IN ONE SURPRISING WAY, EXPERTS SAY

"I had a symptom, which at the time was not that well-known: Acting out your dreams," he said in an Oct. 4 interview with CBS News. "I had a dream that somebody was attacking me. And I picked up a sack of potatoes and threw it at 'em. What I was really doing was throwing a pillow at Arlene, my wife."

Alda identified humor as his way of coping with the frustrations and limitations of the disease.

The actor, pictured with the cast of "M*A*S*H," was diagnosed with the degenerative motor disease in 2015 and publicly shared the news in 2018.  (Getty Images)

While he acknowledged the frustrations of the physical effects and limitations of Parkinson’s, he said "the best way to deal with anything that's a little bit of a problem is to find out what's funny about it and laugh at it."

In one example, he shared that when he has trouble controlling the computer mouse while composing an email, he personifies his condition as "Dr. Parkinson," moving his hand all over the screen and deleting things.

"I don't let Parkinson's define me," Alda said, joking that he sees the disease as "just a hobby."

PARKINSON’S PATIENT’S YEARS-LONG TREMOR VANISHES WITHIN MINUTES OF NEW ULTRASOUND TREATMENT

Rather than wishing he didn’t have the condition, the actor said he aims to accept his current reality.

"I really think reality is my friend," he said. "I don't want to wish it away. I can't wish it away. I can't hope for a better future. I gotta accept what is."

Arlene Alda and Alan Alda attend AARP The Magazine's 19th Annual Movies For Grownups Awards at Beverly Wilshire on Jan. 11, 2020, in Beverly Hills, California. (Getty Images)

Although Alda acknowledged that everyday tasks, such as buttoning his shirt, have become difficult, he said he treats each one like a "puzzle" to solve.

"I do hate it, but the only thing that's helpful is: What haven't I tried? And pretty soon, you get the feeling, 'If I keep looking for new ways to try this, I'll get a solution.' It's a puzzle. Will I be able eventually to put my socks on? The last time I put my socks on was a tremendous moment to celebrate!"

SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISING BRAIN BENEFIT OF LAUGHTER: 'IT'S A MENTAL WORKOUT'

Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, agreed that humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.

"Humor involves cognitive reframing, this idea of looking at a circumstance through different angles — not necessarily changing the reality that one is in, but shifting the meaning and the emotional weight of the situation," an expert said. (iStock)

"Humor involves cognitive reframing, this idea of looking at a circumstance through different angles — not necessarily changing the reality that one is in, but shifting the meaning and the emotional weight of the situation," Lane, who has not treated Alda, told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

When something feels frightening or distressing, such as a medical diagnosis, creating some "psychological distance" can make a "big, big change" in perspective, he added.

Connection is another important component of humor, Lane noted.

"Humor is often shared. It brings us together," he said. "We are meant to share our lives with others. The importance of having a sense of belonging and humor can be a glue in that way, bringing us closer with others so that one does not go on the journey alone."

"Humor is often shared. It brings us together."

Lane shared that he has witnessed the power of humor and connection in his own practice as he cares for people living with Parkinson's disease.

"One of the wonderful things that I've seen in those settings is that, just like Mr. Alda, people crack a joke, [it] brings them a smile."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The neuropsychiatrist also noted that Alda’s acceptance of his condition is "enormously empowering."

"It's the idea of saying to oneself, what are the choices that I can make in the moment?" Lane told Fox News Digital. "Rarely do we ever have control over our entire day and certainly not our entire life, but we often do have control over what we choose in the movement."

"Our sense of agency is an important part of our emotional well-being."

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Democrats debate Kamala Harris 2028 run as surrogate says party wants to 'move on' from 2024 loss
excerpt: Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris discusses her new memoir '107 Days' at the Southbank Centre's London Literature Festival 2025, in London on Thursday Oct. 23, 2025. (Manning/PA Images via Gett...
body_text:
Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris discusses her new memoir '107 Days' at the Southbank Centre's London Literature Festival 2025, in London on Thursday Oct. 23, 2025. (Manning/PA Images via Getty Images)

Allies of former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as Democratic surrogates, are questioning whether the former Democratic nominee would be the top choice within the party, weighing her name recognition and respect among Democrats against the notion that voters want to move on.

"People just want to move on," Fletcher Smith, a former state legislator in South Carolina and Biden 2020 surrogate, told The Washington Post. "We’ve got a number of younger generation of people who are capable of leading — we’ve got governors, we’ve got congresspeople, we have senators. I think what she needs to do is sit out 2028 and let some other people have a shot at saving our democracy."

Many Democratic allies noted Harris is well respected within the party, but questioned whether respect translated into support.

DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028

"She’s extraordinarily popular in the party and people are very fond of her and want her to be treated with a lot of respect and deference — given all the due of someone in her position," Jamal Simmons, a former communications director for Harris, told the Post. "Many people see it as a service what she did in 2024, where she really stepped up for the party, stepped up for Joe Biden, stepped up for the country. There’s a lot of respect for her. But it’s yet to be seen how much of that becomes support for another presidential run."

Kamala Harris allies questioned whether respect within the Democratic Party translates to support for a 2028 presidential election bid. (Getty Images)

Podcast host and former South Carolina state senator Bakari Sellers told the Post that though she is" very talented," she has yet to define what a potential 2028 run would look like to key constituencies.

"One of the first statements she put out was about AI, when it’s clear she needs to boost her support among Black men," Sellers told the Post. "California has a cost-of-living issue, and she’s not talking about cost of living at all."

The Post reported that Sellers said he hasn't spoken to Harris in over a year. He suggested that was concerning for a candidate who would need a victory in South Carolina, according to the report.

HARRIS STOPS IN KEY PRESIDENTIAL PRIMARY STATE AFTER LEAVING DOOR WIDE OPEN TO 2028 RUN

During Sellers' podcast on Monday, he listed Harris as No. 2 in his top five candidates for 2028. He said Harris was talented and intelligent, but questioned whether her team would "let her be great."

"Let Kamala be Kamala, and you would have the next president of the United States without a doubt in my mind," he said. The podcast host ranked Maryland Gov. Wes Moore in the No. 1 spot, calling him the "biggest impediment" to Harris being the nominee.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Joe Biden depart after speaking on the ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas in the Cross Hall of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Jan. 15, 2025. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

WATCH: DEM SENATORS DODGE BACKING KAMALA HARRIS IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN: ‘VERY MESSY’

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, who was part of Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign, told Fox News Digital that Harris hasn't done anything differently since 2024.

"Harris has not done anything truly new or different since 2024. Her greatest post-VP visibility came from her book tour. Running again without a new chapter or story to tell is like reapplying to the same college after getting rejected, taking a gap year, and coming back with basically the same application. You can rewrite the essay, but if you did nothing new, admissions is still looking at the same file," Shroff said.

Shroff suggested somebody new might have the advantage over her because they would be introducing themselves to voters for the first time on a national stage.

"She does not get to reintroduce herself. That is the burden of being so well known. She has a real base and a lot of goodwill in the party, but she also lost, and that makes some voters and, importantly, donors nervous. Even if she starts high in the polls, the question is where the growth comes from if there is not much new to add," he said. "Someone like a Pritzker at least gets the advantage of telling his story to a lot of voters for the first time."

Shroff added, "What Harris is doing well right now is using her position as a party leader rather than acting like a candidate in waiting. A great example is her showing up for Abdul El-Sayed despite his criticism of her and the bad blood with some on the far left in Michigan. She acknowledged the disagreements, still made the case for him, and used her stature to help unite the party in a critical moment — particularly with outreach to Black voters. That is an example of influence she has right now, regardless of what she does in 2028 and that will continue to matter whether she seeks the nomination or not."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom said during a recent interview that he would not run in 2028 if Harris planned to run.

DEM MEGADONOR UNLEASHES REALITY CHECK ON HARRIS FOR 2028 WHILE EYEING SOCIALIST FIREBRAND

Harris has not been definitive on whether she plans to run, but has said she is thinking about it.

Others were more confident in Harris, including Ashley Etienne, another former communications director for the former VP. She told the Post that Harris would need to separate herself from the Democratic establishment, but said she would have major advantages in a national election.

CARVILLE DOESN'T 'FEEL SORRY' FOR URGING DEMOCRATS TO MOVE ON FROM THE KAMALA HARRIS ERA

Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks during the 10th Austrian World Summit climate conference at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna, Austria, on June 16, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

"It’s almost like, why not her? She has proven, unlike anyone else in the race, that she’s got these advantages that will matter in a national election," she told the Post.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Virginia Democratic state senator L. Louise Lucas told the Post that Democrats rejecting Harris too fast could be interpreted as a negative political move as well, suggesting it could be seen as overlooking a qualified Black woman for the position.

"There’s no question that people would be upset because you see what happened last time," Lucas told the Post. "It could very well be that some folks would be so disillusioned that they would just say, ‘I give up on this process’ — especially people who’ve been fighting as many years as I have, who have come through the civil rights movement and just experienced so much, endured so much, and then to see this happen again would be quite painful."

Several members of Congress didn't rush to throw their support behind Harris when asked by Fox News Digital about her possibly running in 2028.

"Well, I've backed her before, but there'll be other contenders this time," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "I've made no decisions about who I would support."

"I think we're going to have a very, very, very messy and very big primary," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said. "It's going to be every Tom, Dick and Harry. And that's probably where it should be."

"We're focused on 2026," said Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md. "We're going to win back the House and the Senate."

She continued, "I love Kamala Harris. I have a very personal friendship and relationship. She's amazing. I think anybody who wants to run should. She's obviously very well qualified. We need to focus on '26."

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

title: Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills
excerpt:
Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers

John Healey is considering a major intervention to cut energy bills for poor...
body_text:
Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers

John Healey is considering a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households at this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed at forecasts which show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January.

The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.

Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether.

Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills.

If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living.

The chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and to rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs.

He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular.

Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year.

But they have become increasingly concerned by forecasts showing that the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut.

As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.

The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.

Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is.

Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies.

Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead.

She told the Guardian last week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it?

“That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.”

Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future.

Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or ones that use less energy.

Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours.

“This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.”

A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones.

Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks.

An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs which energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income.

The idea, which was proposed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level.

Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.”

He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform. This means capturing the benefits of cheap renewables and offering every household a ‘block’ of essential energy at a truly protected and affordable price.”

Alfie Stirling, economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Energy support for this winter needs to tick three boxes. It needs to support the majority of households; within this, it needs to target the most support towards those in greatest need; and – as far as possible – it needs to actually lower the price, thereby bringing down inflation.

“The UK does not yet have the right toolkit to respond effectively to energy price shocks – building better tools is now a critical priority for our future security and living standards.”

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

title: Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death
excerpt:
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case

Russian authorities have denied that they imposed anti-plague measures after a laboratory technician died of suspected pneumonic plague in a case whi...
body_text:
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case

Russian authorities have denied that they imposed anti-plague measures after a laboratory technician died of suspected pneumonic plague in a case which has drawn international scrutiny.

Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague on Friday.

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among staff who had come ⁠into contact with the laboratory worker for the past 10 days.

“This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests,” the watchdog said.

The institute said in a statement that extensive testing during an autopsy on the woman’s body found no microorganisms linked to her work at the anti-plague institute.

It said results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing other infectious diseases had been detected.

Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said no “dangerous diagnosis” had been confirmed.

She added that 60 percent of ⁠those placed under quarantine as a precaution had already been released.

Local media said about 200 people ⁠had previously been quarantined.

US Secretary ⁠of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information on Friday.

“Anytime you hear there is a disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago in 2020 and 2021 when we saw that happen. That said, it would be irresponsible for me to sit here and speculate,” Rubio said.

The World Health Organization in Geneva said on Tuesday that Russia had told it there were no ⁠cases of plague in the city of Irkutsk.

It was unclear if this meant that the laboratory technician’s death was unrelated to plague infection.

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.

Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the WHO.

title: Trump, Waltz link France riots to mass immigration as thousands are arrested
excerpt:
U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz condemns violence in Paris, says open-border and migration policies helped fuel frustration now boiling over across France.

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump...
body_text:
U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz condemns violence in Paris, says open-border and migration policies helped fuel frustration now boiling over across France.

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump warned Tuesday that France’s escalating riots were being driven by "out of control mass migration," as U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz echoed those concerns and blamed unchecked immigration and broader European policy failures for helping fuel the unrest.

Asked by Fox News Digital about Trump’s comments and the scenes emerging from France, Waltz condemned the violence while also linking the unrest to European immigration and economic policies.

"I think we would always condemn lawlessness, condemn the violence that we're seeing in Paris," Waltz told Fox News Digital. "But I think we also have to recognize that when you have open borders, when you [have] this pro-migration, unchecked immigration kind of policy, coupled with policies over the years that deny people basic energy, that overspend on all kinds of other government programs, that you see a level of frustration boiling to the surface."

FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION

Protesters hold a Palestinian flag during demonstrations in Strasbourg France, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026.  (Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters)

Trump weighed in as the unrest intensified, arguing that what was unfolding went beyond the students’ complaints about France’s education system. "What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Tuesday.

"Unfortunately, I think you're seeing the results of some of that, and President Trump has brought that to light," Waltz added.

The comments came as France faced its biggest day of school unrest since the protests began in September. on Tuesday, police fired tear gas in Paris and other major cities, protesters lit fires and hurled projectiles, and France’s Interior Ministry said 6,100 people had been arrested, the overwhelming majority of them minors, according to Reuters. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu describing the clashes as producing the school system’s "heaviest toll in decades".

FRANCE’S VIOLENT STUDENT PROTESTS RAISE WARNING FOR AMERICA: ‘A CAUTIONARY TALE’

FRANCE-POLITICS-EDUCATION-DEMO A protesting student feeds a burnt barrier during a blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on October 1, 2026. Since late September, students have staged protests outside schools over grievances ranging from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year's heatwaves. The protests started in the Ile-de-France region around Paris but have now spread to other cities nationwide. (Photo by LOU BENOIST / AFP via Getty Images) ( )

France’s Interior Ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested so far, the overwhelming majority of them minors. Lecornu told lawmakers Tuesday that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff members have been injured, while his office said more than 700 police officers have also been hurt, according to Reuters.

The latest demonstrations brought clashes in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Rennes, where police fired tear gas as protesters lit fires and hurled projectiles. More than half of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools were blockaded or expected to close Tuesday, according to the High School Students Union. The ⁠Paris police said the clashes there had come about when some 300 people attempted to face off against security forces, adding that the protest was generally unfolding well elsewhere.

Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under Trump, also argued that immigration was contributing to the unrest.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

Masked protesters install a barricade amid clashes with police during a protest by high school students near the Lycee Berthelot high school in Aubervilliers near Paris as part of nationwide protests to demand the hiring of substitute teachers, increased resources and better learning conditions, as more than 400 schools remain closed following days of student protests that have escalated into violence in some places, France, October 2, 2026. The slogan on the placard reads "Same studies, but not the same rights". (Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters)

"The French are notorious for strikes, labor stoppages and street demonstrations. It’s a core part of the Fifth Republic’s civic culture," Wold told Fox News Digital. "What’s new is the violence, lawlessness and rioting. This is a consequence of mass immigration."

While Trump, Waltz and Wold linked the violence to immigration, Reuters and AP have reported that the protest movement began over school conditions, including teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating buildings and education funding. Students have cited overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and deteriorating school buildings — including water leaks and rat infestations — among their grievances.

Students clash with police during ongoing student protest action, in Lyon, central eastern France, on Oct. 1, 2026. Since late September, students have staged protests outside schools over grievances ranging from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year's heatwaves. The protests started in the Ile-de-France region around Paris but have now spread to other cities nationwide. (Alex Martin AFP via Getty Images)

The unrest has increasingly become part of a broader political fight ahead of France’s presidential election in April and May 2027. Reuters reported last week that French authorities and political opponents have accused lawmakers and mayors from the hard-left France Unbowed party, or LFI, of stoking the demonstrations. LFI has denied the accusations.

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond and Reuters contributed to this story.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Former All-Star pitcher 'Sudden' Sam McDowell dead at 84
excerpt:
Scott Spiezio tells Fox News Digital in a recent interview why he opening up about his harrowing descent from World Series hero to nearly dying from jaundice.

Six-time All-Star pitcher Sam McDowell d...
body_text:
Scott Spiezio tells Fox News Digital in a recent interview why he opening up about his harrowing descent from World Series hero to nearly dying from jaundice.

Six-time All-Star pitcher Sam McDowell died Monday at 84.

The cause of death is unknown. KDKA first reported McDowell’s death.

McDowell pitched in the big leagues for 15 seasons, spending 11 of them with the then-Cleveland Indians, parts of two seasons with the San Francisco Giants, parts of two with the New York Yankees and his final season with the Pittsburgh Pirates.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

American baseball pitcher Sam McDowell of the Cleveland Indians poses at Municipal Stadium in Cleveland in July 1969. (UPI/Bettmann Archive/Getty Images)

McDowell, nicknamed "Sudden Sam," won the American League ERA title in 1965 with a dazzling 2.18 ERA and made the first of his six All-Star Games that season. In his career, McDowell had a 141-134 record with a 3.17 ERA in 425 games.

The Pittsburgh native is in the Guardians Hall of Fame. McDowell made his MLB debut at 18 but was out of baseball by 32 in 1975 because of alcohol abuse.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sam McDowell attends the 22nd annual Going to Bat for B.A.T. event at The New York Marriott Marquis on Jan. 25, 2011, in New York City. (Dario Cantatore/Getty Images)

"I was the biggest, most hopeless and most violent drunk in baseball," McDowell told the New York Post in 2001. He recalled jumping off of hotel balconies into swimming pools.

In that same interview, McDowell said he had lost his family and career to alcohol. He went to rehab in 1978 and turned things around. He went back to college and became a licensed therapist in sports psychology and addictions.

Former Cleveland Indians player Sam McDowell attends the Hall of Fame induction ceremony before the game against the Oakland Athletics at Progressive Field in Cleveland, Ohio, on July 30, 2016. (Jason Miller/Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

McDowell then returned to baseball, working for the Toronto Blue Jays and Texas Rangers. From 1987-2016, he served as an addiction and recovery consultant for the Baseball Assistance Team.

"I truly believe with all my heart, the greatest thing that ever happened to me was that I was an alcoholic and found out about it," McDowell said. "Had I never known and had not been thrown out of baseball, I would not have the great life I have now. I would not have the education. I would not have learned how to live and love. Every day is a kick."

Ryan Canfield is a digital production assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Former Obama official will review Cornell’s handling of sexual misconduct complaints
excerpt:
School trustees appoint Sally Yates to review policies as university grapples with fallout from alleged frat gang rape

A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell ha...
body_text:
School trustees appoint Sally Yates to review policies as university grapples with fallout from alleged frat gang rape

A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced on Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.

Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the adequacy of campus police responses, and more.

“It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others,” the trustee chair, Anne Meinig Smalling, said in a statement.

The announcement comes after days of outrage and a large demonstration over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe. She told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.

No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.

Yates will look at how the woman’s complaint was handled and at the oversight of fraternities, sororities and other campus groups, Cornell said.

The woman sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month.

Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by the Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that during an investigation that Cornell conducted under the federal Title IX law, some of the accused students contended that the sexual activity was consensual.

The lawsuit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.

New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter – the review that Yates now will lead.

Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza on Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter and demand more accountability, greater transparency, an overhaul of the disciplinary process and other changes.

Yates had a decades-long career at the justice department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.

She achieved particular prominence in January 2017, when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed justice department attorneys not to defend the constitutionality of Donald Trump’s refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.

Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump’s new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn later was fired.

Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the justice department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.

She led a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women’s Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse.

title: Suspects wanted for stabbing of off-duty NYPD detective are illegal aliens with long criminal histories
excerpt: Illegal migrant Alexis Antonio Cedillos-Campos is arrested for the tragic stabbing of Virginia mother Carmen Lizet Puch on a hiking trail in Great Falls. Former Secret Service agent Charles Marino joi...
body_text:
Illegal migrant Alexis Antonio Cedillos-Campos is arrested for the tragic stabbing of Virginia mother Carmen Lizet Puch on a hiking trail in Great Falls. Former Secret Service agent Charles Marino joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze the suspect's previous release by the Biden administration and demands accountability.

The two suspects wanted for the attempted murder of an off-duty New York City police officer during a robbery have lengthy criminal records and are living in the U.S. illegally, federal officials said.

Dangelo Rafael Jean Caraballo, 25, and Sneider Mejia Bautista, 24, both Dominican citizens, are accused of stabbing off-duty NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes. According to police, the two suspects attempted to snatch Mercedes’ gold chain while he was clearing out the trunk of his car.

He was rushed to the hospital and released this week. Both suspects remain at large.

"This horrific crime could have been prevented if it weren’t for Biden’s open borders and the America Last policies of New York sanctuary politicians," said Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Caraballo’s prior arrests include charges for reckless endangerment, reckless driving, unlawful fleeing from a police officer in a motor vehicle, possession of burglar’s tools, criminal possession of a controlled substance, criminal possession of a weapon involving a loaded firearm and second-degree menacing with a weapon.

An ICE agent monitors hundreds of asylum seekers being processed upon entering the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building on June 6, 2023 in New York City. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images)

Following an October 2025 weapon charge, ICE lodged a detainer against Bautista, but local officials declined the request under New York City's sanctuary policies.

title: The hotel TV privacy mistake that can follow you home
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You've just arrived at your hotel after a long day of travel. The room looks good, the bed looks comfortable and there...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You've just arrived at your hotel after a long day of travel. The room looks good, the bed looks comfortable and there's a big TV on the wall with Netflix and your other favorite streaming apps ready to go. So, you grab the remote, sign in and settle in for the evening. Seems harmless, right?

Here's the part that's easy to forget. That TV was used by plenty of guests before you, and more will use it after you leave. If you sign into a streaming service and forget to log out, your account could still be accessible after you've checked out and headed home. Before you reach for the remote, here's what to know about hotel TV privacy and the safer ways to stream while you're traveling.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better health care.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.

Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.

Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com

TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK

Signing into a streaming app on a hotel TV can leave your account accessible if you forget to log out before checkout. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

A hotel TV isn't your TV at home. It's a shared device that you don't control. When you sign into a streaming service, the app may create and store a session on that television so you don't have to log in every time you turn it on. That doesn't necessarily mean your password is sitting on the TV in plain text. But if the session stays active after you leave, the next person in the room may be able to open the app and use your account.

Depending on the streaming service, that could let someone watch shows using your subscription, switch between profiles or see parts of your viewing activity. Netflix itself warns that a TV from a recent hotel stay can remain connected to your account. Its Manage Access and Devices feature lets you review recently active devices and sign them out remotely.

There is another wrinkle here. Some newer hotel entertainment systems are designed specifically for guests and offer secure casting from your phone instead of requiring you to enter streaming credentials on the TV. Some of these systems automatically disconnect your device when you check out. That's a much better setup when it's available. Still, you can't assume every hotel TV works that way.

Smart TVs can also collect information about what's being watched. Some television platforms use technology called Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to identify content displayed on the screen and collect viewing information. The exact tracking depends on the TV, its software and its privacy settings.

That doesn't mean every hotel television is tracking you personally or connecting your Netflix identity to everything you watch. Hotel TVs can use specialized commercial software and configurations that work differently from the smart TV sitting in your living room. But it's another reason I wouldn't treat a hotel television like one of my personal devices.

FLORIDA SUES NETFLIX, ALLEGES STREAMER TRACKED CHILDREN AFTER PROMISING FAMILIES PRIVACY

If the hotel supports secure casting or HDMI, you can watch on the big screen without signing directly into the TV. (D.A. Varela/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

My preference is simple: keep your streaming accounts on devices you control. Your phone, tablet or laptop already has your streaming apps and account information. If you want to watch on the larger hotel screen, first check whether the hotel offers a casting option that lets you connect from your own device without entering your password on the TV.

If it doesn't, an HDMI cable can be another option. Connect your laptop to the TV and switch the television to the correct HDMI input. Depending on your phone or tablet, you may also need a compatible USB-C or other video adapter. HDMI carries audio, video and certain control signals between devices, but connecting your laptop this way generally does not give the hotel TV access to the passwords, documents or other personal files stored on your computer. One caution: some hotel TVs have locked inputs or hotel equipment connected to the HDMI ports. If you disconnect anything to use the port, put it back exactly as you found it before you check out.

Hotel Wi-Fi deserves some attention too, although there's an important distinction here. Most major websites and streaming services use HTTPS encryption, which means your password and other information aren't simply sitting out in the open for another hotel guest to read.

Still, you're connecting through a network you don't control. A VPN adds another layer of privacy by encrypting the connection between your device and the VPN server. If you use a VPN when traveling, turn it on before connecting to sensitive accounts or doing other private browsing. A VPN service can help reduce what the hotel network or Wi-Fi operator can see about your internet traffic. Just remember that a VPN doesn't make you invisible online. The streaming service you're using still knows you're connected to it.

For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

BEFORE YOU CONNECT ANOTHER SMART TV, TABLET OR PHONE, LOCK IT DOWN

Using your own phone, tablet or laptop keeps your streaming credentials on a device you control. (iStock)

If you're reading this from your hotel room and you're signed into Netflix or another streaming service on the TV, there's no reason to panic. Before you leave, open the streaming app and choose Sign Out. Don't assume that closing the app or turning off the TV signs you out. If you've already checked out and can't remember whether you logged out, do this:

Look in your streaming service's account or security settings for recently active devices. Netflix has a Manage Access and Devices section that lets you remotely sign out individual devices.

If you see a device you don't recognize or one that appears to be the hotel TV, remove it.

Check profiles and viewing activity for anything you don't recognize.

Use a strong, unique password for that streaming account. A password manager can help you create and store a long, random password so you don't have to reuse one from another account. If you're changing a Netflix password, keep the Sign out all devices option selected so existing sessions are removed.

Some streaming accounts use verification codes or other additional checks for certain sign-ins and account changes. Turn on any additional account protection your service provides.

I've stayed in enough hotels to know how tempting it is to drop your bag, turn on the TV and sign straight into Netflix. But I don't like putting my account credentials into a device I don't own, especially when I have other options sitting right in my bag. If the hotel offers secure casting from your phone, that's the first thing I'd look for. Otherwise, I'll use my own laptop or mobile device and connect to the television when possible. I also like using a VPN on hotel Wi-Fi for an added layer of privacy on a network I don't control. And if you do sign directly into that hotel TV, add one thing to your checkout routine: log out before you walk out the door. It takes a few seconds and could save you from discovering days later that somebody else is still enjoying your streaming account.

Have you ever checked into a hotel and found someone else's streaming account still signed in on the TV? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain after warrant lifted
excerpt:
EU Parliament lifts immunity of 3 Catalans, including Puigdemont

Self-exiled Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont could be set to return to Spain after the country’s Constitutional Court ruled...
body_text:
EU Parliament lifts immunity of 3 Catalans, including Puigdemont

Self-exiled Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont could be set to return to Spain after the country’s Constitutional Court ruled that an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applies to embezzlement charges against Puigdemont.

A Supreme Court judge then lifted a warrant for Puigdemont’s arrest on Tuesday, clearing the way for his return without fear of arrest.

Puigdemont, then president of Catalonia, fled to Belgium in 2017 after holding an independence referendum for his self-governing region to break away from Spain. Madrid said the vote was illegal.

Catalonia unilaterally declared independence from Spain that year after the referendum, with 90 percent of voters backing independence.

He has since avoided several extradition attempts by Spain to face trial over the vote, while many of his confidants and supporters spent time in prison.

Members of Puigdemont’s political party Junts welcomed his potential return.

“It’s a great victory for President Puigdemont and the two other exiled ‌[leaders in Belgium]”, Jordi Turull, secretary-general of Junts, told reporters.

“They held firm, they resisted, they prevailed in Europe, and today they have prevailed against the Spanish state.”

Puigdemont appears set to return to Spain just as the country is preparing for a snap election in November, although an official from his Junts party said he is unlikely to take part.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was only able to remain in power in 2023 when Puigdemont’s Junts party, along with another Catalan party, backed his new government in exchange for the amnesties.

A year ago, Junts withdrew its support for the minority central government, and the party was decisive in Spain’s progressive government losing two key votes in parliament this week when it tried to push through emergency housing measures amid street protests.

Sanchez responded by calling a November snap election, hoping anger over housing will mobilise his voters.

The prime minister told ⁠reporters on Tuesday he did not regret launching the amnesty and welcomed the court ruling.

“I believe the important message is that of coexistence among Catalans,” he said.

Although separatism has lost ground and Junts is trailing in opinion polls, Puigdemont’s return could prompt renewed political drama.

Spain’s conservative People’s Party is leading in opinion polls ahead ‌of the election and may need to seek the support of Junts and other centre-right parties to govern.

title: Senior academics set out key questions Cambridge must answer over Jason Arday’s death
excerpt:
Letter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before death

Senior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s plans to investig...
body_text:
Letter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before death

Senior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s plans to investigate Prof Jason Arday’s death as inadequate, and said those responsible for “serious failures of leadership” should face consequences.

In a letter to Chris Smith, Cambridge’s chancellor, the academics said “it is not yet clear” how the proposed review will answer difficult questions about the university’s involvement in the events leading up to Arday’s death, including its handling of the criticism Arday suffered after his appointment as professor of sociology of education in 2023.

Arday died at his home in London on 14 August, nine days after he resigned amid allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.

An inquest will be held to determine the cause of death.

Arday’s family said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.

Now, a letter signed by more than 40 professors, associate professors and fellows raises concern that Cambridge has backed away from initial promises by Deborah Prentice, the university’s vice-chancellor, to carry out a “thorough and transparent” examination of the circumstances that led to Arday’s appointment and treatment.

Rather than reviewing the “lessons learned”, the group wants the investigation to pinpoint the crucial advice given and decisions made during Arday’s hiring and subsequent career.

“The investigation must establish who authorised and directed the university’s public promotion of Professor Arday; what assessment was made of the risks that accompanied it; who authorised any legal or other communications with journalists investigating the story; what the university knew as racist and ableist abuse and media hounding escalated; and how responsibility for Professor Arday’s protection was allocated and exercised across the university,” the letter says.

The signatories included Cahir O’Kane, a professor of genetics; Caroline Bassett, a professor of digital humanities; Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature; and Clément Mouhot, a professor of mathematical sciences.

Cambridge last month announced a two-part review, with part one to be led by Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, focusing on the support given to Arday immediately before his death.

The university has not yet named a chair for part two of the review, which it said would be “a broader review of institutional processes and practice” and only consider “the wider context” of Arday’s period at Cambridge, including general appraisals of recruitment and support available to academics facing media scrutiny.

The group behind the letter, which was also sent to Cambridge’s governing council, said the “scope and investigative character” of the second part of the review would be crucial in settling the decisions, structures and processes involved.

They wrote: “To this end, it is vital that the university establishes a clear chain of responsibility for the institutional decisions made in the period following Professor Arday’s appointment, through the events leading to his death and the university’s subsequent responses.

“The university should state clearly how responsibility will be acted upon if the review establishes serious failures of leadership or responsibility … Serious findings must have consequences for the individuals and offices responsible.

“At the same time, individual accountability cannot substitute for the institutional changes required where failures arose from structures of decision-making, scrutiny or governance.”

The University of Cambridge was approached for its response to the letter.

Cambridge publicised Arday’s appointment at the age of 37 as the youngest black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university, saying he would “inspire more people from under-represented backgrounds into higher education, building on the university’s many initiatives in this area”.

Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but on 5 August Cambridge said it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours later.

title: California couple charged with child abuse in surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 children
excerpt:
Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan had 15 children, aged between two months to 13 years, removed from their home

A California couple has been arrested on child abuse charges following an investigation into...
body_text:
Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan had 15 children, aged between two months to 13 years, removed from their home

A California couple has been arrested on child abuse charges following an investigation into a surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 kids, police said on Tuesday.

Silvia Zhang and her husband, Guojun Xuan are expected to face conspiracy to commit child abuse charges, according to the Los Angeles county sheriff’s department.

Fifteen children were removed from the couple’s opulent home in Arcadia last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from two months to 13 years, with most between one and three.

Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children while the rest were born by surrogate.

Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their two-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of a nanny at the home violently shaking the baby, according to Arcadia police.

Arcadia police did not file charges at the time, in order to finish a full investigation, they said.

The couple told police that they “wanted a large family” and produced what appeared to be legitimate birth certificates, including some from outside California, that list Zhang as the mother of the children. Xuan was listed as the father on at least some of the birth certificates.

Surrogacy is an agreement between parties to have a woman become pregnant, typically through an embryo transfer and deliver a baby for another parent.

The practice has no federal regulation, leaving it up to states to set the rules if they choose to allow it.

California is considered a “surrogacy-friendly state” because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.
